headline: Arkansas medical marijuana cards top 120,000 for the first time
dek: The Arkansas Department of Health counted a record 120,075 active medical marijuana cards on 21 November 2026, even as first-half sales slipped.
key_points: Arkansas had 120,075 active medical marijuana cards as of 21 November 2026, the first count above 120,000, according to the state health department.
That is about 8.6% more than the 110,539 cards reported in July 2025, on our arithmetic.
Patients bought a record $291.1 million in 2025, but first-half 2026 sales fell 2.6% to $140.3 million, Talk Business & Politics reported.
Federal rescheduling of medical marijuana and a state court ruling letting lawmakers amend the program set up a busy 2027 session.
body: Arkansas now has more registered medical marijuana patients than at any point since its program began. The Arkansas Department of Health's medical marijuana page lists 120,075 active cards as of 21 November 2026, the first time the count has passed 120,000. The Marijuana Herald, which first reported the milestone, put the gain at about 5,000 cards since 1 June.

Growth in patients has not translated into growth in spending this year. Dispensary sales in the first six months of 2026 were slightly lower than a year earlier, according to state figures reported by Talk Business & Politics, as prices fell and patients near the borders shopped elsewhere.

The card count has risen steadily. Talk Business & Politics reported 110,539 active cards in July 2025, 115,113 in January 2026, 119,074 in July 2026 and 119,013 in September 2026. On those figures, today's count is about 8.6% higher than in July 2025 and about 1,060 higher than in September.

The Herald's June baseline of 115,073 sits below the July 2026 figure Talk Business reported, so month-to-month counts appear to move around as cards are issued and expire. The year-on-year trend is the clearer signal: steady growth of several thousand patients a year.

Arkansas voters approved the medical marijuana amendment in November 2016, by 53% to 47%, and the first dispensary, Suite 443 in Hot Springs, opened on 10 May 2019. The program covers 17 qualifying conditions and lets patients buy up to 2.5 ounces every 14 days. Adult-use marijuana remains illegal. From 1 October 2026 the health department charges caregivers a $50 application or renewal fee and a $40 background check.
> Arkansas keeps adding patients, but each one is spending a little less: the program's growth is in headcount, not dollars.
## Sales: a record year, then a soft half

Patients bought $291.1 million of medical marijuana in 2025, a record and 5.5% more than in 2024, Talk Business & Politics reported in January. December 2025 was the best month on record at $25.7 million. The state collected $32.3 million in taxes in 2025, and more than $1.6 billion of product has been sold since sales began.

The first half of 2026 was weaker. Sales from January to June totaled $140.3 million, down 2.6% from $144 million a year earlier, with an average purchase of $75.14. Tax collections, which come from the 6.5% state sales tax and a 4% privilege tax on sales from cultivators to dispensaries, were flat at $16.8 million. The Herald reports that patients bought $165 million through July; we could not match that figure to a state release.

The count of shops has edged down. Talk Business reported 36 licensed dispensaries in the first half of 2026, down from 37, with one Texarkana licensee closed. A Rogers dispensary operator told the outlet in September that falling revenue reflects price compression and competition from adult-use markets in neighbouring Missouri and Oklahoma.

Put the numbers together and the pressure is visible. If patient numbers are up by high single digits year on year while first-half sales fell, average spending per patient is falling. That squeezes dispensaries even as the customer base grows.

Two developments will shape the program in 2027. First, federal rescheduling: the order moving state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III took effect in April, and Talk Business reported in September that it lets Arkansas medical operators deduct cost of goods sold on federal taxes, relief from the Section 280E penalty that has applied to Schedule I businesses. For thin-margin dispensaries, that may matter more than sales growth.

Second, the state's own law is now easier to change. In December 2025 the Arkansas Supreme Court ruled that lawmakers can amend citizen-initiated constitutional amendments with a two-thirds vote, overturning decades of precedent, in a case that arose from legislative changes to the medical marijuana amendment, the Arkansas Advocate reported. Senate President Pro Tempore Bart Hester said lawmakers could amend but not repeal the program and that changes would likely wait for the 2027 session. Marijuana tax revenue now funds free school breakfasts.

Federal gun rules are also in play for patients. As we report in this edition, ATF says it is still reviewing a draft Form 4473 that would stop treating medical marijuana patients as unlawful drug users.

The Arkansas General Assembly convenes in January 2027, the first regular session since the Supreme Court ruling, and any changes to purchase limits, licensing or taxes would come there. Watch also the health department's monthly card count, the state's full-year 2026 sales figure in January, and whether federal tax relief slows dispensary closures.
